prompt:
# Write one principle card

You are writing a **principle card**: one mechanism, stated so precisely that
somebody who has never seen your sources could implement it and somebody else
could prove it wrong.

The card is not the implementation. A later step turns it into a behaviour-tree
leaf, and that step will be given **your card and nothing else** — not this
prompt, not your reasoning, not whatever you were given below. So everything the
implementer needs has to survive inside the six fields.

## The system the principle has to fit

A Unitree Go2 quadruped navigating an indoor space it has no map of. Below the
behaviour tree sits an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy: the
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`, saturated
to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and `|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Nothing you write touches the
policy, the gait or the joints.

What the robot can sense, once per control step:

```
t                    sim seconds since the episode started
ranges               181 lidar beams over a full circle, metres, inf where no return
range_angles         beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
range_max            6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
pose_estimate        (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, never ground truth
pose_error_estimate  scalar metres — how wrong we believe that belief is
contact              bool — are we touching something right now
goal                 (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of those are traps. `pose_estimate` **drifts** on some scenarios — a seeded
random walk is added to it — and ground truth is never observable. `goal` may be
`None`, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still scored against it but
this robot has not found it yet; it latches once seen.

## The task family this principle has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is NOT disclosed. `obs.goal` is None until the robot has been close enough to see the goal with nothing in the way, after which it latches. Until then the task is to cover ground that has not been covered, in an indoor space with no map.

<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK BEGIN ---- -->
## What to base the principle on

The full text of a published paper is reproduced below. Read it and extract the
principle it establishes.

```
[PAPER TEXT REDACTED FROM THIS TRANSCRIPT — 17359 characters, sha256(pdf)=e9f40cbbd48ac1a9, extractor=cache. The corpus is an input and is never committed (out/corpus/ is gitignored). The prompt_hash recorded beside this is the hash of the REAL prompt, so a machine holding the PDF re-renders it byte-identically and replay finds this transcript.]
```

Work from the document, not from your memory of it. Where the two disagree, the
document wins. Quote its own threshold, exponent or closed form where it states
one, and put the section, page or equation number in `span` so somebody else can
check it.

The paper was written about something other than a quadruped with a planar
lidar. Carrying it across is the `derivation` field's whole job: say what in the
original maps onto what here, and say plainly where the mapping is yours rather
than the paper's.
<!-- ---- SOURCE BLOCK END ---- -->

## What a card is

Six fields. `mechanism`, `trigger` and `derivation` are prose. `prediction` is
**structured**, because a prediction that cannot be decided automatically cannot
become a unit test — and this one will be run as one, with no human in the loop.

```yaml
id: <short_snake_case_identifier>
node_name: <TheLeafThisWouldProduce>       # CamelCase, verb-first

source:
  citation: <the reference this principle comes from, or the single line
             "(no source - the principle was devised, not extracted)" if it
             comes from none>
  span: <the section, page, figure or equation number where the mechanism is
         stated — the part that makes a threshold checkable. LEAVE EMPTY if you
         cannot point at a location you are sure of.>

mechanism: <what happens, and why it helps. The finding, not the implementation.>
trigger: <the condition under which it applies -> becomes the precondition port>
derivation: <how that becomes a rule for THIS robot and THESE sensors. Numbers
             belong here, with their units, and so does the reasoning that got
             you to them.>

prediction:
  statement: <the falsifiable claim, in words>
  metric: <what gets better>
  baseline: <goal_seeker or reactive_avoid>
  min_effect: <a number: the smallest effect that would count as support>
  cost_metric: <the metric this mechanism is expected to make WORSE>

confidence: <high | medium | low>
```

### `prediction.metric` — the closed list

The metric must be one the scorer actually computes, and one a **controller can
move**. These and no others:

| metric | better |
|---|---|
| `goal_reached` | higher (a rate over seeds) |
| `spl` | higher (path efficiency) |
| `min_clearance` | higher (closest approach to anything, metres) |
| `collisions`, `near_misses` | lower |
| `stuck_events`, `time_stuck`, `recovery_time` | lower |
| `time_to_goal`, `path_length` | lower |

`localisation_failures`, `optimal_distance`, `scenario` and `seed` are **not
available**: no controller can move them, so a prediction naming one is not
falsifiable about the node and the card is rejected at load.

`cost_metric` is the honest counterpart — the metric this mechanism is expected
to make worse. A mechanism that buys clearance with time should say so. It may
be empty only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs nothing, and you
should be suspicious of that belief.

### `confidence` — criteria about the SOURCE, not about how sure you feel

- **high** — the mechanism *and* its quantitative form are stated explicitly in
  a source you can point at; the span points at the equation, threshold or
  exponent itself.
- **medium** — the mechanism is stated explicitly somewhere, but the
  quantitative form is adapted: different units, a different body scale, a
  different sensor. The number is yours; the mechanism is not.
- **low** — the mechanism is qualitative and the derivation is entirely yours.
  Still usable, but it is your claim, and the card must not read otherwise.

## Rules

- **One mechanism.** A card describing two is two cards. This is not a style
  rule: the unit scenario that decides admissibility has to isolate one claimed
  effect, and it cannot isolate two.
- **No coupling to a specific scenario.** The leaf will run on worlds nobody has
  seen. The card may not name a room, a coordinate, a doorway or a map.
- **Do not invent a `span`.** An empty span is a result and costs nothing. A
  section number reconstructed from the shape of such papers is a fabrication,
  it will be checked against the document, and it is the single failure this
  pipeline exists to detect.
- **Do not invent numbers.** If a source states a threshold, an exponent or a
  closed form, give it and say where. If it does not, derive one, say the
  derivation is yours, and set `confidence: low`.

## What to return

One fenced ```yaml block containing exactly one card, and nothing else that
looks like YAML. Prose outside the fence — including, if it applies, an honest
statement of what you did not know.

response.text:
```yaml
id: ant_path_integration_outbound_bearing
node_name: SteerAlongAntOutboundVector

source:
  citation: >
    Müller, M. & Wehner, R. (1988) "Path integration in desert ants, Cataglyphis
    fortis." Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 85:5287-5290.
  span: >
    Results, "Two-Leg Trajectories", p. 5288, Eqs. 1a, 1b and 2, and Eq. 3
    (phi_{n+1} = phi_n + k(180+d)(180-d)d / l_n); the fitted constant
    k = 4.009 x 10^-5 deg^-1 and the 90-degree normalisation cap are stated in
    the first paragraph of p. 5289. Error-cancellation and the "sharp backward
    turns" failure mode: Discussion, p. 5289, first paragraph.

mechanism: >
  A foraging ant does not vector-sum its outbound path. It carries exactly two
  running scalars - a mean direction phi_n (the bearing from the nest along
  which it reckons it has travelled) and an accumulated length l_n in stride
  units - and updates them incrementally as a distance-weighted running mean:
  phi_{n+1} = [phi_n*l_n + (phi_n + d)] / (l_n + 1), l_{n+1} = l_n + 1 - d/90deg
  (Eqs. 1a, 1b), which for l >> 1 stride collapses to phi_{n+1} = phi_n + d/l_n
  (Eq. 2), and which fits the ants' measured homing errors over the full turning
  range only in the form phi_{n+1} = phi_n + k(180deg + d)(180deg - d)d / l_n
  with k = 4.009e-5 deg^-1, the product being normalised so it maximally reaches
  90 degrees (Eq. 3, p. 5288-5289). Two properties make this worth stealing, and
  neither is accuracy. First, the update is purely idiothetic: it consumes only
  self-motion (one unit advance, one turn angle d) and never an external
  position fix, so it cannot inherit the error of any position estimate. Second,
  the division by l_n makes the direction estimate anneal itself: early steps
  swing phi hard, and once l_n is large a single turn barely moves it, so the
  agent's committed outbound bearing stiffens automatically with distance
  travelled, with no tuned time constant. The l-update is a turn-discounted
  odometer - a 90-degree turn cancels a whole unit of advance and a reversal
  subtracts one - so l_n measures ground genuinely gained away from the start,
  not path walked. Steering to hold the robot's heading on phi_n (i.e. directly
  away from the reckoned start point) therefore produces long, straight,
  self-lengthening outbound excursions rather than a diffusive random walk,
  which is what covering unseen indoor area cheaply requires. The paper's own
  defence of the approximation applies here: its errors are large only for sharp
  backward turns, which are rare, and left/right errors are equal and opposite
  so they cancel unless turns are strongly one-sided (Discussion, p. 5289).

trigger: >
  The accumulator runs on every control step of the episode unconditionally,
  from t = 0, whichever leaf holds the tree - it is state, not an action. The
  leaf's precondition port fires only when all of: (a) obs.goal is None, i.e.
  the goal has not yet been seen and latched, so the task is still coverage;
  (b) the accumulated turn-discounted length satisfies l_n >= 6 strides
  (~0.5 m) so phi_n is defined and not dominated by the first few ticks;
  (c) at least one lidar bearing inside +-90 deg of the desired robot-frame
  heading is admissible (see derivation). If (c) fails the port returns false
  and the tree falls through to whatever recovery or avoidance leaf sits to its
  right; this leaf never handles obstacle emergencies itself.

derivation: >
  Mapping. Ant stride -> one fixed 10 Hz accumulator tick (dt = 0.1 s), chosen
  by me because the control rate is not specified; accumulate the commanded
  Twist and fire the update when sim time t has advanced by >= 0.1 s. Ant unit
  length -> u = 0.08 m, the distance covered in one tick at the |vx| <= 0.8 m/s
  saturation limit; l_n stays dimensionless (strides), so reckoned distance from
  start is l_n * u metres. Ant celestial compass + odometer -> the commanded
  (vx, vy, wz) themselves, NOT pose_estimate: pose_estimate is a drifting belief
  with a seeded random walk added, and the ant's system reads no such external
  fix, so the transfer is only faithful if the integrator is fed self-motion.
  Concretely, per tick: s_n = hypot(vx, vy) * dt metres, d_n = degrees(wz * dt)
  signed, and an idiothetic heading psi_{n+1} = psi_n + d_n (psi_0 = 0). Ant
  nest -> the robot's pose at t = 0; phi_n is then the reckoned bearing from
  that origin to the robot, in the same idiothetic frame as psi, so the
  difference phi_n - psi_n is a robot-frame bearing that stays correct even as
  both scalars drift together. This same-frame-difference argument is mine; the
  paper has no drifting external estimate to contrast against.
  Numbers. Update l_{n+1} = l_n + s_n/u - |d_n|/90, clamped to l_n >= 1. I read
  the "d/90" discount of Eq. 1b as using |d|, because signed d would make a left
  turn lengthen the home vector, which the paper's geometry cannot mean; the
  absolute value is my reading. Update phi with the paper's Eq. 3 verbatim,
  phi_{n+1} = phi_n + k*(180 + d_n)*(180 - d_n)*d_n / l_n with
  k = 4.009e-5 deg^-1, all angles in degrees, the increment clipped to +-90 deg
  per the paper's normalisation, phi wrapped to (-180, 180]. At this robot's
  limits |wz| <= 1.0 rad/s gives |d_n| <= 5.73 deg per tick, so
  (180 + d)(180 - d) ~= 32400 deg^2 and Eq. 3 reduces to
  phi_{n+1} = phi_n + 1.299 * d_n / l_n: within the Go2's turn-rate saturation
  the ant's full model is Eq. 2 with a fixed gain of 1.299, i.e. the outbound
  bearing swings about 30% more per degree turned than the paper's simpler Eq. 2
  and about 1.30*(1 + 1/l_n) times more than an exact vector sum. That overshoot
  is the ant's systematic error, kept deliberately: for choosing "which way is
  away" a few degrees of bias is irrelevant, and per p. 5289 it cancels over
  balanced left/right turning. The 1.299 reduction is arithmetic of mine on the
  paper's constant.
  Output. Desired robot-frame heading theta* = wrap(radians(phi_n) - psi_n_rad).
  A lidar bearing theta_i is admissible if ranges[i] >= 1.5 m (treat inf as
  range_max = 6.0 m) and every beam within +-0.35 rad of it reads >= 0.6 m.
  Among admissible bearings with |wrap(theta_i - theta*)| <= 90 deg pick the one
  minimising |wrap(theta_i - theta*)|; call it e. Command
  wz = clip(1.5 * e, -1.0, 1.0) rad/s, vx = 0.8 * max(0, cos e) * min(1, (d_e -
  0.6)/1.4) m/s where d_e is the range along the selected bearing, vy = 0. If
  obs.contact is true, or the forward 30 deg sector reads < 0.6 m, emit
  vx = 0 and let the port go false on the next tick. If goal latches non-None
  the leaf stops emitting; the accumulator keeps running. The 1.5 m / 0.6 m /
  0.35 rad / 1.5 gain / 6-stride numbers are mine, sized from Go2 body width
  ~0.31 m plus margin and the 0.8 m/s, 1.0 rad/s saturations; the paper states
  none of them.

prediction:
  statement: >
    On unmapped indoor scenarios where obs.goal is None until seen, a leaf that
    holds heading on the ant integrator's outbound bearing phi_n (Eq. 3, fed
    only by commanded twist) reaches the goal on a larger fraction of seeds than
    a reactive_avoid baseline, because turn-discounted displacement from the
    start grows monotonically and self-stiffens with distance instead of
    diffusing; the advantage must persist on scenarios where pose_estimate
    drifts, since the integrator never reads it.
  metric: goal_reached
  baseline: reactive_avoid
  min_effect: 0.15
  cost_metric: min_clearance

confidence: medium
```

What I did not know, stated plainly:

- **Control rate.** The spec gives one observation per control step but never its frequency, so I fixed my own 10 Hz accumulator tick and derived the unit length `u = 0.08 m` from it plus the `0.8 m/s` saturation. If the real step rate differs, `u` and the stride count change but every formula above is unaffected.
- **An OCR garble in Eq. 1b.** The reproduced text prints the second update as `In+1 = In + 1 - in` with a stray `8900` on the preceding line. I read it as `l_{n+1} = l_n + 1 - d/90°`, which is the only reading consistent with the surrounding prose and with Eq. 2 following from Eq. 1a. I also take the discount on `|d|` rather than signed `d`; the paper does not say so explicitly and that choice is mine.
- **The paper is about a walking insect with a celestial compass and no rangefinder.** Everything about lidar admissibility, the 1.5 m / 0.6 m gates and the twist mapping is mine. The paper contributes exactly two things to this card: the pair of update equations with `k = 4.009 × 10⁻⁵ deg⁻¹`, and the empirical claim that the resulting errors are tolerable except on sharp backward turns.
- **The direction of the transfer is inverted relative to the paper's subject.** Ants use `phi + 180°` to get home; I use `phi` itself to keep going away from home. That inversion is mine, and it is the reason the mechanism's known inaccuracy is affordable here — nothing in this card depends on the home vector being metrically right.
